findings.where: First screen, the action row under the second paragraph (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The row shows two identical solid blue buttons, 'Write to me' and 'Book a consultation', with the email address set between them. Neither button wins, so the screen has no single primary action. Because the address sits the same distance from both buttons, it reads as belonging to either one. On desktop it even looks like the label for 'Book a consultation'. The row reads as a choice between two equal routes rather than one personal way to reach Mark.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer ready to make contact would pause to work out which button is the real way to reach Mark, and what the address belongs to. The founder would object too: the brief asks for one action on the first screen and one direct, personal way to reach him.

findings.where: Phone, the hero's action row (phone-01, bottom of the tinted band)
findings.fault: The row breaks apart when it stacks. The address wraps under 'Write to me' with almost no gap before the 'Book a consultation' button, which crowds it from below. That second button is also indented about 16 px from the left edge that every other hero element shares. As a result the address and the two buttons look like a stray pile rather than an aligned group.
findings.who_objects: A visitor on a phone looking for how to get in touch meets the one ragged, misaligned spot on an otherwise tidily aligned column. That reads as unfinished, at the very moment the page asks for trust.

findings.fault: On phone the stacking order puts the photograph, its two-line caption, an eight-line block of tracked capitals and two margin notes between Mark's line and the action. The way to reach him lands near the end of the second phone screen, so the first screen has the message but no action.
findings.who_objects: Most first visits from busy agency staff happen on a phone. A visitor who reads the line and wants to act has to scroll past the photo and the whole introduction to find any contact.

findings.where: Header, the logo lockup at the top left (desktop-01 and phone-01)
findings.fault: 'MMM INFRA' under the arches sits almost on the header's bottom edge, where the tinted hero band begins. There is almost no space below it, yet ample space above it. Mark's name to its right hangs from the top while the nav sits lower, so the three header items share no line.
findings.who_objects: Mark and the founder, looking at his logo first: a lockup that looks clipped by the band below it and out of line with the nav makes the header look unsettled, on a page that otherwise sells restraint and precision.

findings.where: First screen, the photograph column on the right (desktop-01)
findings.fault: The framed photograph floats in the right column. Its top does not line up with the heading's first line or with the paragraph, and its caption does not line up with the action row. It sits between them, aligned to nothing in the text column, which weakens the editorial grid this direction depends on.
findings.who_objects: The founder, judging the 'well-set brief' direction: the point of v3 is a page that looks typeset. An exhibit placed without reference to the text's lines looks dropped in rather than set.

findings.where: Motion section, below the curve (desktop-04 to desktop-05)
findings.fault: The exhibit photo and the timing table start lower on the right, beside 'Placed. Settled. Still.', while the left column stops after the curve's caption. This leaves a block about 400 px tall of empty paper on the left, under the curve, while the right column carries the photo, link and table. The section feels lopsided and the two halves look unrelated.
findings.who_objects: The founder, reviewing the motion sketch: the gap makes the section look like two separate pieces, so the reader can't tell at a glance that the curve, the photo and the table describe one entrance.

findings.where: Article specimen, the download row on phone (phone-03 to phone-04)
findings.fault: The Download button keeps its place beside the title, so the lecture title is squeezed into a narrow column of four short lines, with the button stranded at the top right. The row loses the clean title-then-meta reading it has on desktop.
findings.who_objects: Angélique and the visitors she publishes for: the PDF list is the product the brief names, and on phone each entry would become a cramped, uneven block, harder to scan down a list of lectures.
